analysis.one_liner: Narrows the legal standard for when big brands and staffing firms count as workers' joint employers.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in January 2022 with no cosponsors, was placed on the Senate calendar, and never received a Senate vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Federal labor laws can hold two companies jointly responsible for the same workers — for example, a fast-food brand and the local franchisee, or a big company and the staffing agency that supplies its temps. This bill would rewrite that 'joint employer' standard so a company only counts as a joint employer if it directly, actually, and immediately controls essentials like hiring, firing, pay, day-to-day supervision, schedules, and discipline [S2][S3]. That would make it much harder to hold the bigger, richer company responsible when a smaller contractor or franchisee shortchanges workers [S2][S3]. The bill never got a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: If it had passed, the main winners would be large franchisors — fast-food chains, hotel brands, cleaning and delivery companies — and staffing or contracting agencies, which would be shielded from joint legal responsibility for wages, overtime, and workplace conditions at the businesses that actually employ the workers [S2][S3].

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the broader joint-employer test with a narrow one: a company is only a joint employer if it directly, actually, and immediately exercises significant control over hiring, firing, pay and benefits, day-to-day supervision, scheduling, and discipline [S2][S3].

Applies the same narrow standard to both the National Labor Relations Act (which governs union rights) and the Fair Labor Standards Act (which governs minimum wage, overtime, and child labor), so workers could rarely reach the bigger company under either law [S3].
Under this standard, a brand that sets menu prices, uniforms, and systems — but not individual pay and schedules — would generally not be responsible for a franchisee's labor-law violations [S2].

analysis.who_pays: If it had passed, workers at franchises, contractors, and staffing agencies would bear the cost: if the smaller employer failed to pay minimum wage or overtime, broke union rules, or provided unsafe conditions, they could generally pursue only that smaller employer, not the big company behind it [S2][S3].

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection is that joint-employer liability can leave small franchisees and local contractors facing legal responsibility for standards set by the big brand, and the bill would return that responsibility to the smaller business that employs the workers day to day [S2].

The cost an honest supporter would acknowledge: under the bill's direct-control test, workers who are shorted on wages or fired for organizing would usually have no claim against the larger company even when that company effectively sets the terms of the job through its brand standards [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would simplify compliance for local businesses, but its main effect would be shifting risk off large franchisors and staffing firms and onto the workers with the least bargaining power, since those companies could keep deep operational control while escaping legal responsibility for pay and conditions. Weighed honestly, the cost to workers outweighs the convenience benefit to the businesses shielded by it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced, placed on the Senate calendar in mid-January 2022, and never brought to the floor for a vote before the Congress ended in January 2023 [S5][S1].

narrative.text: Sen. Roger Marshall introduced the bill on January 10, 2022, with no cosponsors [S1][S4].
It was read twice and placed on the Senate Legislative Calendar under General Orders on January 18, 2022 (Calendar No. 245), where it remained [S5][S1].
No committee was listed, no vote was ever scheduled, and the bill died when the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S5][S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Workers at franchise and contracting businesses, who kept the broader joint-employer protections that would have been narrowed; the bill's target industries avoided nothing because it never became law, but also risked nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Workers who kept the broader joint-employer rules

for.name: Sen. Roger Marshall
for.role: U.S. Senator from Kansas; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and had it placed on the Senate calendar, but drew no cosponsors

against.name: Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote in the nearly two years it sat on the calendar

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken; the bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors from either party [S4][S5].

industries.industry: Franchisors (fast-food chains, hotel and service brands)
industries.note: The bill would have shielded them from joint responsibility for wages and conditions at franchise locations even where the brand sets the systems workers operate under, shifting that risk to workers. The bill died, so they gained nothing, but this is the industry it was written to protect [S2][S3].
Agencies supplying workers to bigger companies would rarely count as joint employers under the direct-control test, limiting joint liability when those workers are shorted on pay [S2][S3].
Under the National Labor Relations Act, the narrow standard would have made it harder to bargain with or hold accountable the big company that shapes a subcontractor's workplace [S3].
A narrower joint-employer test makes it harder to treat platforms that control work through apps as employers of the people doing the work, reducing their wage-and-hour exposure [S2].
